topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks over six questions, sat every Summer. A diagram part opens a longer mechanics question and is worth 2 marks; Summer 2025 carried three of them in one paper. The marks are among the cheapest in the paper and the reports say about half the entry drops one of them, so the two marks are worth more attention than their size suggests.
mustMemorise: Weight = mg, vertically downwards from the centre of the body; g = 10 m/s²
One normal reaction per contact, at right angles to the surface
Tension acts along the string, away from the body; one string, one letter
Friction acts along a rough surface, against the sliding; a smooth surface gives none
Every force needs an arrow and a label, and nothing else goes on the diagram
Each body of a connected pair gets its own complete set of forces
notOnThisSpec: The coefficient of friction and F = μR: CCEA gives the frictional force itself, as a number or as so many newtons per kilogram of mass
Limiting equilibrium and the idea of a force being on the point of moving
Air resistance, lift and drag on a moving body
g = 9.8 m/s²: this unit takes g = 10 m/s², as the front page of every FM2 paper states

mustBeAbleTo: Name every force acting on a body and show each one as an arrow with a label
Draw the weight mg vertically downwards from the centre of the body, on the flat and on a slope
Draw one normal reaction per contact, at right angles to the surface
Draw the tension along each string, away from the body, with one letter per string
Draw friction along a rough surface, against the sliding, and none at all on a smooth one
Give each body of a connected pair its own complete set of forces
Leave masses, components of the weight, velocities and accelerations off the diagram
Work out a weight from a mass, and a force given in newtons per kilogram from the mass
sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2. A diagram part opens a longer mechanics question and is worth 2 marks: Summer 2025 had three of them (Q4(i) two blocks over a pulley, Q5(i) a suspended rod, Q6(i) a box on a rough slope), Summer 2024 Q4(iii) a box on a slope, Summer 2023 Q4(i) a pulley pair. The scheme splits the 2 marks as any half of the forces, then the rest, and the later parts of the question are marked follow-through from the diagram the candidate drew.
traps: The normal reaction is left off the block altogether, the commonest omission of all (Summer 2022 Q3(b)(i), Summer 2025 Q6(i))
Friction points the way the body is moving, or is missing from a rough surface (Summer 2025 Q4(i), Summer 2025 Q6(i))
Arrowheads or labels are missing, so a force that is drawn earns nothing (Summer 2019 Q3(i))
The two ends of one string take different letters, or two different strings share one (Summer 2019 Q4(i))
The weight is not drawn vertically on a slope, or not from the centre of the body (Summer 2024 Q4(iii), Summer 2019 Q4(i))
Extra forces are invented: a second reaction on one surface, or the pull down the slope drawn as a force of its own (Summer 2024 Q4(iii), Summer 2022 Q3(b)(i))
A weight is labelled with the mass in kilograms instead of mg in newtons (Summer 2025 Q4(i))
The reaction is written down as the weight, without resolving (Summer 2023 Q3(i))

noteBlocks.lede: Before any mechanics question can be answered the forces have to be found and named. A force diagram is that list, drawn: one arrow for every push or pull on the body, each with a label. Get the picture right and the equations almost write themselves.
can: Name every force acting on a body and show it as a labelled arrow
Place weight, normal reaction, tension and friction correctly, on the flat and on a slope
Decide what belongs on a force diagram and what does not, on one body, two joined bodies or a rod

noteBlocks.md: Push a book across a table and four forces act on it: the Earth pulls it down, the table pushes it up, your hand pushes it along and the table drags it back.

noteBlocks.text: 1. A force: a size and a direction

noteBlocks.alt: A crate of mass 14 kg on a rough floor, pulled by a rope at 30 degrees above the floor. Four arrows leave the crate: R straight up, 140 N straight down, T up to the right along the rope, and F to the left along the floor.

noteBlocks.caption: Four forces on a crate, each an arrow with a label.

noteBlocks.md: A force is a vector, with a size and a direction. Each force is drawn as a straight arrow from the body, pointing the way it acts, labelled with its size or its letter. Speeds, accelerations and masses never go on the diagram.
**Shown, for the crate:** its mass is 14 kg, so the Earth's pull is $14 \times 10 = 140$ N, drawn straight down and labelled 140 N, not 14 kg.

noteBlocks.prompt: On the force diagram above, the arrow pointing straight down from the crate is labelled 140 N. Which force is it?
options: the weight of the crate
the mass of the crate
the normal reaction on the crate
noteBlocks.explain: The Earth pulls the crate down with $14 \times 10 = 140$ N, as in the line above: that is its weight. A mass would be in kilograms, and is not a force at all.

noteBlocks.md: Drop a body and nothing touches it: the only force on it is its weight, and it falls with acceleration $g$. Newton's second law, $F = ma$, then says the weight is $m \times g$. This paper takes $g = 10$ m/s², so every kilogram weighs 10 newtons.
**Shown:** a 2.5 kg bag falls freely, so $W = ma = 2.5 \times 10 = 25$ N. Its mass stays 2.5 kg; the force it causes is 25 N.

noteBlocks.prompt: A sack has a mass of 17 kg. Taking $g = 10$ m/s², what is its weight, in newtons?
noteBlocks.explain: $W = mg$, as for the bag above: $17 \times 10 = 170$ N. The mass is in kilograms; the weight it causes is in newtons.

noteBlocks.text: 3. Weight points down, even on a slope

noteBlocks.alt: A box of mass 18 kg resting on a slope inclined at 20 degrees, with its weight of 180 N drawn straight down from its centre, not down the slope.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 146.3L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 69.2 254.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>20°</text><path d='M162.2 220.4L229.8 195.8L212.7 148.8L145.1 173.5Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='187.4' y='179.6' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>18 kg</text><path d='M187.4 184.6L187.4 256' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M187.4 256L183.2 246L191.6 246Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='195.4' y='254' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>180 N</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: Tilt the surface and the weight does not tilt with it.

noteBlocks.md: The Earth pulls towards its centre whatever the surface is doing, so the weight arrow is vertical on a floor and still vertical on a slope, drawn from the centre of the body. The 2024 report saw weights that were not drawn vertically.

**Shown, for the box in the picture:** $18 \times 10 = 180$ N.
**Direction:** straight down from its centre; the slope's $20°$ changes nothing about it.

noteBlocks.prompt: A box of mass 18 kg rests on a slope. A student draws its weight as an arrow of 180 N pointing down the slope, parallel to the surface. What is wrong?
options: The direction: the weight acts vertically downwards
The size: it should be 18 N
Nothing: on a slope the weight acts down the slope
noteBlocks.answer: The direction: the weight acts vertically downwards
noteBlocks.explain: The size is right, $18 \times 10 = 180$ N, but the Earth pulls straight down, as in the picture, whatever the slope. The pull down the slope is only part of the weight, found later; it is not the weight's direction.

noteBlocks.text: 4. Why the reaction is at right angles

noteBlocks.alt: A box on a slope inclined at 30 degrees, with the normal reaction R leaving it at right angles to the slope.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 73.7L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 65.8 247' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>30°</text><path d='M164.8 189.9L227.2 153.9L202.2 110.5L139.8 146.5Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M171 128.5L142 78.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M142 78.3L150.6 84.9L143.4 89.1Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='134' y='80.3' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>R</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: On a slope the reaction R is at right angles to the slope, not to the ground.

noteBlocks.md: A surface cannot pull; it can only push back on a body pressing into it. Anything along the surface is friction, a separate force with its own label.

noteBlocks.title: Why the push is at right angles
noteBlocks.md: The surface pushes only because the body is trying to sink into it, and sinking in is a movement straight into the surface. So the push that stops it comes straight back out, at right angles.
**Shown, on a 30° slope:** the reaction is at $90°$ to the surface, so it makes $90° - 30° = 60°$ with the ground, and $90° - 60° = 30°$ with the vertical: the slope's own angle.

noteBlocks.prompt: A box rests on a slope inclined at 40° to the horizontal. What angle does the normal reaction on the box make with the vertical, in degrees?
noteBlocks.explain: The reaction is at right angles to the slope, as in the line above, so it makes $90° - 40° = 50°$ with the ground and $90° - 50° = 40°$ with the vertical: the slope's own angle.

noteBlocks.text: 5. Friction: along the surface, against the sliding

noteBlocks.alt: A block of mass 4 kg sliding down a rough slope inclined at 30 degrees: R at right angles to the slope, 40 N straight down, friction F up the slope, and a dashed arrow showing the motion down the slope.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 73.7L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 65.8 247' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>30°</text><path d='M164.8 189.9L227.2 153.9L202.2 110.5L139.8 146.5Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='183.5' y='145.2' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>4 kg</text><path d='M214.7 132.2L264.9 103.2' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M264.9 103.2L258.3 111.8L254.1 104.6Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='257.4' y='89.1' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>F</text><path d='M171 128.5L142 78.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M142 78.3L150.6 84.9L143.4 89.1Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='134' y='80.3' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>R</text><path d='M183.5 150.2L183.5 228.2' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M183.5 228.2L179.3 218.2L187.7 218.2Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='191.5' y='226.2' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>40 N</text><path d='M117.4 123.7L82.8 143.7' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><path d='M82.8 143.7l5.9 -9.8M82.8 143.7l11.4 -0.2' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><text x='92.1' y='123.8' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>a</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: The block slides down, so friction F acts up the slope.

noteBlocks.md: Friction acts along the surface and against the sliding: a block sliding down a slope has friction pointing up it, and turning the motion round turns friction round. A rough surface gives friction; a smooth one gives none. This paper gives friction as a value or in newtons per kilogram.

**Shown, for the block:** 2 N per kilogram on 4 kg is $2 \times 4 = 8$ N.
**Direction:** the block slides down, so friction is drawn up the slope.

noteBlocks.prompt: A block slides down a rough slope. In which direction does the force due to friction on the block act?
options: up the slope
down the slope
vertically upwards
noteBlocks.explain: Friction opposes the sliding, as for the block above: it slides down, so friction acts up the slope, along the surface.

noteBlocks.md: **Per kilogram again:** 0.5 N per kilogram on a 30 kg crate is $0.5 \times 30 = 15$ N: the rate times the mass, never the weight.

noteBlocks.prompt: The force due to friction on a crate of mass 22 kg is 1.5 N per kilogram of its mass. What is the force due to friction, in newtons?
noteBlocks.explain: The rate times the mass, as in the line above: $1.5 \times 22 = 33$ N. Multiplying by the weight, 220 N, would give ten times too much.

noteBlocks.text: 6. Tension: a string pulls along itself

noteBlocks.alt: A lamp of mass 2.5 kg hanging at rest from a vertical cable: the tension T up along the cable and the weight 25 N straight down.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 290' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='290'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='154' y='123' width='92' height='54' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='200' y='156' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16' font-weight='600'>2.5 kg</text><path d='M200 18V123' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.6'/><path d='M200 123L200 59' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M200 59L204.2 69L195.8 69Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='210' y='71' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>T</text><path d='M200 177L200 241' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M200 241L195.8 231L204.2 231Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='210' y='239' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>25 N</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: A cable can only pull, so its tension points up along it.

noteBlocks.md: A string, rope or cable can only pull, never push, so its tension acts along the string, away from the body. A body hanging still from one cable has just two forces: its weight down and the tension up, and they balance.

**Shown, for the lamp:** its weight is $2.5 \times 10 = 25$ N, down.
**The cable:** $T$ acts up along it, and at rest $T = 25$ N.

noteBlocks.prompt: A lamp of mass 1.2 kg hangs at rest from a single vertical cable. What is the tension in the cable, in newtons?
noteBlocks.explain: Two forces act, as on the lamp above: the weight, $1.2 \times 10 = 12$ N, down, and the tension up along the cable. At rest they balance, so $T = 12$ N.

noteBlocks.text: 7. Two bodies, two sets of forces

noteBlocks.alt: A block of mass 10 kg on a rough table joined by a light string over a smooth pulley at the table's edge to a block of mass 2 kg hanging below. Both parts of the string are labelled T, and friction F acts on the table block, away from the pulley.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 222' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='222'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='16' y='92' width='232' height='116' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.05'/><path d='M16 92H248V208' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><rect x='78' y='46' width='88' height='46' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='122' y='74.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>10 kg</text><circle cx='268' cy='83' r='14' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><circle cx='268' cy='83' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M268 83L248 104' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><path d='M166 69L268 69' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><path d='M282 83L282 142' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><rect x='254' y='142' width='56' height='46' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='282' y='170.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>2 kg</text><text x='217' y='61' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>T</text><text x='291' y='120.5' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>T</text><path d='M78 77L32 77' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M32 77L42 72.8L42 81.2Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='55' y='63' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>F</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: One string, one tension T: the same label at both ends.

noteBlocks.md: When two bodies are joined, each gets its own complete set of forces. The block on the table has a reaction and friction; the hanging block has neither, because it touches nothing. A light string over a smooth pulley carries one tension all along, so both ends take the same label $T$.

**Shown, the 10 kg block:** $10 \times 10 = 100$ N, $R$, $T$ and $F$: four forces.
**The 2 kg block:** $2 \times 10 = 20$ N and $T$: two forces.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two blocks are joined by a light string passing over a smooth pulley. The tension pulling one block is labelled T. What label should the tension pulling the other block carry?
noteBlocks.explain: One string carries one tension, as on both blocks above, so the same letter is used at both ends. A second string would need a second letter.

noteBlocks.text: 8. See it done: work round the body

noteBlocks.alt: A box of mass 24 kg pulled up a rough slope inclined at 28 degrees by a rope along the slope: T up the slope, F down the slope, R at right angles to the slope and 240 N straight down.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 89.2L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 66.6 248.4' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>28°</text><path d='M164.2 196.5L227.8 162.7L204.3 118.6L140.7 152.4Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='184.3' y='152.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>24 kg</text><path d='M216 140.6L267.3 113.4' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M267.3 113.4L260.4 121.8L256.5 114.4Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='260.5' y='99' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>T</text><path d='M152.5 174.4L101.3 201.7' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M101.3 201.7L108.1 193.3L112.1 200.7Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='87.4' y='187.2' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>F</text><path d='M172.5 135.5L145.3 84.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M145.3 84.3L153.7 91.1L146.3 95.1Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='137.3' y='86.3' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>R</text><path d='M184.3 157.5L184.3 235.5' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M184.3 235.5L180.1 225.5L188.5 225.5Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='192.3' y='233.5' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>240 N</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: Earth, surface, string, sliding: four forces, four arrows.

noteBlocks.md:
**A 24 kg box pulled up a rough slope by a rope along it.**
**Earth:** the weight, $24 \times 10 = 240$ N, straight down.
**Surface:** the normal reaction $R$, at right angles to the slope.
**String:** the tension $T$, up the slope along the rope.
**Sliding:** the box moves up, so friction $F$ acts down the slope.

noteBlocks.title: Force diagrams
noteBlocks.why: The same four forces put on several bodies in turn. Watch how each arrow is drawn from the body and labelled before any arithmetic starts.

noteBlocks.prompt: A crate is pulled up a rough slope by a rope parallel to the slope. How many forces act on the crate?
noteBlocks.explain: Work round it as above: the Earth gives the weight, the surface the normal reaction, the rope the tension and the sliding the friction, down the slope. Four forces, four arrows.

noteBlocks.title: On the diagram, and never on it
noteBlocks.md:
**On:** the weight in newtons, one reaction per contact, one tension per string, friction on a rough surface.
**Never:** a mass in kilograms, a second reaction on one surface, a part of the weight drawn again, a velocity or an acceleration.

noteBlocks.title: What the reports keep saying
noteBlocks.md: About half the entry misses one of the two diagram marks: a reaction left off, friction the wrong way round, or a force that was never there.
**Shown:** on a 30° slope, $60\sin 30° = 60 \times 0.5 = 30$ N of a 60 N weight acts down the slope (the resolving topic finds it); those 30 N are already inside the 60 N arrow.

noteBlocks.prompt: A box rests on a rough slope. Which one of these should not be drawn as a force on the box?
options: the component of the weight down the slope
the normal reaction
the force due to friction
noteBlocks.answer: the component of the weight down the slope
noteBlocks.explain: That component is part of the weight, as the line above showed, and the weight is already on the diagram. Drawing it as well counts the same pull twice.

noteBlocks.md: **The other forces** (2019, 2021, 2022). Part of the diagram is printed, usually the pull. Mark only the forces that are missing, and do not draw the printed one again.
**Smooth or rough** (2019 to 2025). The word decides whether friction is drawn at all. **Two blocks** (2022, 2023, 2025): each gets its own set, and the hanging one has only its weight and $T$.
**Shown:** a 1.5 kg block on a smooth table with its pull printed: add the weight, $1.5 \times 10 = 15$ N, and the reaction $R$. Smooth, so no friction.

noteBlocks.prompt: A block on a smooth horizontal table is pulled by a string, and the pull is already printed on the diagram. Which forces do you add?
options: the weight and the normal reaction
the weight, the normal reaction and friction
the weight, the normal reaction and the pull again
noteBlocks.answer: the weight and the normal reaction
noteBlocks.explain: The table is smooth, so there is no friction, and the pull is printed already, as in the line above: only the weight and the normal reaction are missing.

the weight
the normal reaction

noteBlocks.md: Every Summer paper since 2019 asks for all the forces on a rod. A uniform rod's weight acts at its midpoint; each support pushes up with its own reaction; each string pulls with its own tension, two strings taking two letters. The 2019 report saw the weight placed halfway between the strings.

**Shown:** the rod's weight is $8 \times 10 = 80$ N, at M, $4 \div 2 = 2$ m from A.
**With it:** the 50 N load, $R$ at C and $T$ at B: four forces.

noteBlocks.prompt: A uniform rod hangs horizontally from two vertical strings, and a block hangs from one end of it. How many forces act on the rod?
noteBlocks.explain: Count as for the rod above: its own weight at the midpoint, one tension for each string (two letters), and the pull of the block's string at the end. Four forces.

noteBlocks.md:
Draw every force as a labelled arrow, the weight as mg in newtons.
Place the weight vertically and the reaction at right angles to the surface.
Turn friction against the sliding, and give one string one tension label.
Give each body of a joined pair, and a rod, its own complete set of forces.
Leave off masses, components and anything that is not a push or a pull.

The opening part of a mechanics question asks you to show every force on the body, on a diagram already printed for you, and it carries two marks: one for roughly half the forces, one for the rest. The first mark is for arrows pointing the right way with labels; the last is for having them all and nothing extra. Stuck? Work round the body: Earth, surface, string, sliding.

workedExamples.stem:
A crate of mass $6$ kg is pulled along a rough horizontal floor by a rope. The rope makes an angle of $26°$ with the floor.

(i) Name the four forces acting on the crate.
(ii) Write down the weight of the crate.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 290' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='290'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M20 199H380' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M24 207l8 -8M36 207l8 -8M48 207l8 -8M60 207l8 -8M72 207l8 -8M84 207l8 -8M96 207l8 -8M108 207l8 -8M120 207l8 -8M132 207l8 -8M144 207l8 -8M156 207l8 -8M168 207l8 -8M180 207l8 -8M192 207l8 -8M204 207l8 -8M216 207l8 -8M228 207l8 -8M240 207l8 -8M252 207l8 -8M264 207l8 -8M276 207l8 -8M288 207l8 -8M300 207l8 -8M312 207l8 -8M324 207l8 -8M336 207l8 -8M348 207l8 -8M360 207l8 -8M372 207l8 -8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='0.9' stroke-opacity='0.5'/><rect x='104' y='145' width='92' height='54' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='150' y='178' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16' font-weight='600'>6 kg</text><path d='M196 168L302.1 116.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2.2'/><path d='M302.1 116.3L294.9 124.4L291.2 116.9Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='310.1' y='114.3' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'></text><path d='M196 168H258' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3 3' stroke-opacity='0.7'/><path d='M234 168A38 38 0 0 0 230.2 151.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='244.7' y='161.8' text-anchor='start' font-size='14'>26°</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: A crate of mass 6 kg on a rough horizontal floor, with a rope attached to its side at 26 degrees above the floor.

steps.working: The weight is drawn vertically from the centre: $W = 6 \times 10 = 60$ N.
steps.decision: Start with the Earth, because the weight is on every diagram and never depends on what else is happening.

options: Because every body on the Earth has a weight, whatever it is resting on
Because the crate is moving, so it must have a weight
Because the floor is rough, so the weight is larger
whyMenu.explain: Weight depends only on the mass and on $g$. Motion and roughness change other forces, never the weight.

steps.working: The crate touches the floor, so the floor pushes back: the normal reaction $R$, straight up out of the floor.
steps.decision: Work round the body in order — Earth, then surfaces, then strings, then sliding — so nothing is forgotten.

options.text: the normal reaction $R$, straight up out of the floor
options.feedback: The floor pushes straight out of itself, and on a level floor that is vertically up.

options.text: the normal reaction $R$, along the floor against the pull
options.feedback: A surface pushes straight out of itself. A force along the floor is friction, which is the last force in the list.

options.text: no reaction, because the rope lifts the crate off the floor
options.feedback: The rope lifts only part of the weight. The crate still presses on the floor, so the floor still pushes back.

steps.working: The rope pulls along itself, away from the crate: the tension $T$, at $26°$ to the floor.
steps.decision: A string pulls and never pushes, so the arrow leaves the crate along the rope.

options.text: the tension $T$, along the rope at $26°$ to the floor
options.feedback: A rope pulls along its own line, away from the body it is tied to.

options.text: the tension $T$, horizontally along the floor
options.feedback: A rope pulls along its own line. This rope is tilted at $26°$, so its tension is tilted too.

options.text: the tension $T$, and a second force dragging the crate forwards
options.feedback: One rope gives one force. The forward drag is part of the tension, not a second force.

steps.working: The floor is rough and the crate slides forwards, so friction $F$ acts backwards, along the floor.
steps.decision: Friction needs a rough surface and a direction of sliding. Both are given, so it is drawn against the motion.

options.text: friction $F$, backwards along the floor
options.feedback: The crate slides forwards over a rough floor, so friction acts backwards, against the sliding.

options.text: friction $F$, forwards, the way the crate is moving
options.feedback: Friction works against the sliding, so it points the opposite way to the motion.

options.text: no friction, because the rope pulls harder than friction
options.feedback: A rough floor gives friction whenever the crate slides. The size of the pull decides whether the crate speeds up, not whether friction is there.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (i) weight, normal reaction, tension and friction  (ii) $60$ N

workedExamples.stem:
A box of mass $9$ kg is held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at $24°$ to the horizontal by a rope lying along the slope.

(i) Name the forces acting on the box.
(ii) State the direction of each one.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 118.6L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 68 251.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>24°</text><path d='M163.1 209L228.9 179.7L208.6 134L142.8 163.3Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='185.8' y='166.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>9 kg</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: A box of mass 9 kg on a smooth slope inclined at 24 degrees. A rope lying along the slope holds it at rest.

steps.working: Vertically downwards from the centre of the box: weight $= 9 \times 10 = 90$ N.
steps.decision: Tilting the surface does not tilt the Earth's pull, so the weight arrow stays vertical.

steps.working: Normal reaction $R$, at right angles to the slope.
steps.decision: The surface pushes straight out of itself, so on a slope that is perpendicular to the slope, not vertical.

options: Because the only push a surface makes is the one that stops the box sinking into it
Because the reaction always balances the weight exactly
Because the box is at rest, so every force must be vertical
whyMenu.explain: Sinking in would be movement straight into the surface, so the push that prevents it comes straight out. On a slope the reaction is smaller than the weight.

options.text: the normal reaction $R$, at right angles to the slope
options.feedback: The slope pushes straight out of itself, so the reaction is perpendicular to the slope.

options.text: the normal reaction $R$, vertically upwards
options.feedback: Vertically up is the reaction on a level floor. On a slope the push tilts with the surface.

options.text: the normal reaction $R$, up the slope
options.feedback: Along the slope is where the rope pulls. The slope itself can only push straight out of its surface.

steps.working: Tension $T$, up the slope, along the rope.
steps.decision: The rope pulls away from the box along its own line, and here that line is the slope.

options.text: the tension $T$, up the slope along the rope
options.feedback: The rope lies along the slope and pulls the box towards where it is tied, up the slope.

options.text: the tension $T$, vertically upwards
options.feedback: A rope pulls along its own line, and this rope lies along the slope.

options.text: the tension $T$, down the slope
options.feedback: A rope can only pull the box towards whatever it is tied to. It is holding the box up, so it pulls up the slope.

steps.working: No friction: the slope is smooth.
steps.decision: Smooth means the surface offers nothing along itself, so drawing friction would be inventing a force.

options.text: no friction, because the slope is smooth
options.feedback: A smooth surface gives nothing along itself, so nothing else is drawn.

options.text: friction $F$, up the slope
options.feedback: The slope is smooth, so there is no friction. Drawing it would invent a force, which costs a mark.

options.text: friction $F$, down the slope
options.feedback: The slope is smooth, so there is no friction in either direction. Only the rope acts along the slope.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Weight $90$ N vertically down, reaction $R$ at right angles to the slope, tension $T$ up the slope, and no friction

twin.stem: A box of mass $9$ kg is held at rest on a smooth slope by a rope parallel to the slope. Which force does not act on it?

options.text: friction
options.feedback: A smooth surface gives no friction, so nothing is drawn along the slope except the rope's tension.

options.text: the normal reaction
options.feedback: The box touches the slope, so the slope pushes back at right angles to itself.

options.text: the weight
options.feedback: Every body on the Earth has a weight, and it acts vertically down whatever the surface does.

workedExamples.stem:
A block of mass $5$ kg rests on a rough horizontal table. A light inextensible string joins it over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table to a block of mass $8$ kg hanging freely.

Name all the forces acting on each block.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 222' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='222'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='16' y='92' width='232' height='116' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.05'/><path d='M16 92H248V208' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><rect x='78' y='46' width='88' height='46' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='122' y='74.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>5 kg</text><circle cx='268' cy='83' r='14' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><circle cx='268' cy='83' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M268 83L248 104' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><path d='M166 69L268 69' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><path d='M282 83L282 142' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><rect x='254' y='142' width='56' height='46' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='282' y='170.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>8 kg</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: A block of mass 5 kg on a rough horizontal table, joined by a light string over a smooth pulley at the table's edge to a block of mass 8 kg hanging freely.

steps.working: On the $5$ kg block: the normal reaction $R$ up, and the weight down, $5 \times 10 = 50$ N.
steps.decision: Deal with one body at a time. This one rests on the table, so it has a reaction as well as its weight.

steps.working: On the $5$ kg block: tension $T$ towards the pulley, friction $F$ away from the pulley.
steps.decision: The string pulls the block towards the pulley, and the table is rough, so friction opposes that pull.

options.text: tension $T$ towards the pulley, and friction $F$ away from the pulley
options.feedback: The string pulls the block towards the pulley, and friction on the rough table opposes that pull.

options.text: tension $T$ towards the pulley, and friction $F$ towards the pulley as well
options.feedback: Friction works against the pull of the string, so it points away from the pulley.

options.text: tension $T$ towards the pulley, and no friction
options.feedback: The table is rough, so friction acts on the block, against the pull of the string.

steps.working: On the $8$ kg block: tension $T$ up, and the weight down, $8 \times 10 = 80$ N.
steps.decision: The hanging block touches nothing, so it has no reaction and no friction: two forces only.

options: Because a normal reaction needs a surface in contact, and the hanging block has none
Because the hanging block is lighter, so it needs fewer forces
Because the string already includes the reaction
whyMenu.explain: A reaction is a surface pushing back. Nothing is touching the hanging block, so nothing pushes it.

steps.working: The same letter $T$ is used at both ends of the one string.
steps.decision: The string is light and the pulley smooth, so the tension does not change along it.

options.text: the same letter $T$ at both ends of the string
options.feedback: A light string over a smooth pulley carries one tension, so one letter serves both ends.

options.text: a different letter at each end, such as $T_1$ and $T_2$
options.feedback: Different letters are for different strings. One light string over a smooth pulley has one tension all the way along.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: $5$ kg block: $50$ N, $R$, $T$, $F$.  $8$ kg block: $80$ N and $T$.

twin.stem: A different block, of mass $13$ kg, hangs freely from a light string. Write down its weight, in newtons.

Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the question-and-answer booklet

workedExamples.stem:
A parcel of mass $2$ kg is on a rough slope inclined at $20°$ to the horizontal.

(i) The parcel slides down the slope. Name the forces acting on it, with their directions.
(ii) It is then pulled back up the slope at a steady speed by a string parallel to the slope. Name the forces acting on it now.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 146.3L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 69.2 254.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>20°</text><path d='M162.2 220.4L229.8 195.8L212.7 148.8L145.1 173.5Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='187.4' y='179.6' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>2 kg</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: A parcel of mass 2 kg on a rough slope inclined at 20 degrees.

steps.working: In both parts the weight is drawn vertically down from the centre: $W = 2 \times 10 = 20$ N.
steps.decision: Start with the Earth: the weight is the same whichever way the parcel moves.

steps.working: In both parts the slope pushes back: the normal reaction $R$, at right angles to the slope.
steps.decision: One contact gives one reaction, straight out of the surface, whatever the motion.

options.text: the normal reaction $R$, at right angles to the slope
options.feedback: The slope pushes straight out of itself, so the reaction is perpendicular to it in both parts.

options.text: the normal reaction $R$, vertically upwards
options.feedback: Vertically up is the reaction on a level floor. On a slope it tilts with the surface.

options.text: no reaction while the parcel is sliding
options.feedback: The parcel presses on the slope whether it moves or not, so the slope always pushes back.

steps.working: (i) The parcel slides down over a rough surface, so friction $F$ acts up the slope.
steps.decision: Friction needs a rough surface and a direction of sliding; it points against the sliding.

options.text: friction $F$, up the slope
options.feedback: The parcel slides down, so friction opposes that and acts up the slope.

options.text: friction $F$, down the slope
options.feedback: That is the way the parcel is moving. Friction acts against the sliding.

options.text: a force down the slope as well as friction
options.feedback: The pull down the slope is part of the weight, which is already drawn. Only friction is added.

steps.working: (ii) The string adds the tension $T$, up the slope along the string; the parcel now slides up, so friction $F$ turns round and acts down the slope.
steps.decision: Redraw for the new motion: a new string brings a new force, and friction always faces the sliding.

options: Because friction opposes the sliding, and the parcel now slides up the slope
Because the string pulls friction round with it
Because friction always acts down a slope
whyMenu.explain: Friction depends on the direction of sliding. Going down it points up the slope; going up it points down. The weight and the reaction do not change.

options.text: tension $T$ up the slope, and friction $F$ down the slope
options.feedback: The string pulls along itself, up the slope, and friction now opposes sliding up the slope.

options.text: tension $T$ up the slope, and friction $F$ still up the slope
options.feedback: Friction faces the sliding. The parcel now moves up, so friction points down the slope.

options.text: tension $T$ up the slope, and no friction at a steady speed
options.feedback: A rough surface gives friction whenever the parcel slides, at a steady speed or not.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (i) weight $20$ N vertically down, normal reaction $R$ at right angles to the slope, friction $F$ up the slope  (ii) weight $20$ N, $R$, tension $T$ up the slope, friction $F$ down the slope

twin.stem: A sack of mass $21$ kg is dragged up a rough slope by a rope parallel to the slope. In which direction does the force due to friction on the sack act?

options.text: down the slope
options.feedback: The sack slides up, so friction opposes that and acts down the slope.

options.text: up the slope
options.feedback: That is the way the sack moves. Friction acts against the sliding.

options.text: at right angles to the slope
options.feedback: At right angles to the slope is the normal reaction. Friction lies along the surface.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: which of these is a vector quantity?

options.text: force
options.feedback: A force has a size and a direction, which is why it is drawn as an arrow.

options.text: mass
options.feedback: Mass has a size only. It is measured in kilograms and points nowhere.

options.text: time
options.feedback: Time has a size only.

options.text: distance
options.feedback: Distance has a size only; displacement is the vector version.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: taking $g = 10$ m/s², what is the weight of a body of mass $5$ kg?

options.feedback: That is the mass with newtons written after it.
That divides by $g$ rather than multiplying.
That uses $g = 9.8$, which this unit does not.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a line is drawn at right angles to a surface. What angle does it make with that surface?

options.feedback: Right angles and $90°$ are the same thing.
That is half a right angle.
That is a straight line along the surface and back.
That would lie flat along the surface.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a quantity is drawn on a diagram as an arrow. What does the arrowhead show?

options.text: the direction in which the quantity acts
options.feedback: The arrowhead carries the direction; the label carries the size and the name.

options.text: the size of the quantity
options.feedback: The size is written beside the arrow as a label.

options.text: the point the quantity acts at
options.feedback: That is where the arrow starts, not where it ends.

options.text: the unit the quantity is measured in
options.feedback: The unit belongs in the label.

items.stem: A sledge is pulled across rough snow by a rope. A force diagram shows its weight, the normal reaction and the tension. Which force is missing?

options.text: friction, backwards along the snow
options.feedback: The snow is rough and the sledge slides, so friction acts against the sliding.

options.text: a second normal reaction
options.feedback: One surface gives one reaction, and it is drawn already.

options.text: a forward force keeping it moving
options.feedback: The forward pull is the tension, already drawn. Nothing else pushes the sledge along.

options.text: none: the diagram is complete
options.feedback: Rough snow and a sliding sledge always mean friction.

items.stem: A crate is being pushed to the right across a rough floor. In which direction does the force due to friction on the crate act?

options.text: to the left, along the floor
options.feedback: Friction opposes the sliding, so it points against the motion, along the surface.

options.text: to the right, along the floor
options.feedback: That would help the crate along. Friction always works against the sliding.

options.text: vertically upwards
options.feedback: That is the normal reaction. Friction acts along the surface, not out of it.

options.text: vertically downwards
options.feedback: Downwards is the weight's direction. Friction lies along the surface.

items.stem: Which of these could be the label on an arrow in a force diagram?
items.skill: What an arrow is labelled with

options.feedback: A force is measured in newtons, so a size in newtons can label its arrow.
Kilograms measure mass, which is not a force. The weight of 45 kg would be 450 N.
An acceleration is not a force, so it never goes on a force diagram.
A velocity is not a force either.

items.stem: A box rests on a slope inclined at $35°$ to the horizontal. What angle does the normal reaction make with the surface of the slope?

options.feedback: The reaction always leaves the surface at right angles, whatever the slope.
$35°$ is the slope's angle to the ground. The reaction is at right angles to the slope itself.
$55°$ is the angle a vertical reaction would make with this slope, and the reaction is not vertical here.
A force along the surface is friction. The reaction pushes straight out of it.

items.stem: A box rests on a slope inclined at $30°$ to the horizontal. In which direction does its weight act?

options.text: vertically downwards
options.feedback: The Earth's pull does not tilt with the surface. The weight stays vertical.

options.text: down the slope
options.feedback: Part of the weight acts down the slope, but that part is a component, not the weight itself.

options.text: at right angles into the slope
options.feedback: That is the direction of the other component of the weight, and the opposite of the reaction.

options.text: at $30°$ to the vertical
options.feedback: The angle of the slope changes the components of the weight, never its direction.

items.stem: A crate hangs from a crane by a cable. In which direction does the tension in the cable act on the crate?

options.text: up along the cable, away from the crate
options.feedback: A cable can only pull, so its tension acts along it, away from the body it is tied to.

options.text: down along the cable, into the crate
options.feedback: That would be the cable pushing. A cable can only pull, away from the crate.

options.text: vertically down, the same way as the weight
options.feedback: The weight already points down. The cable holds the crate up, so its pull is upwards along the cable.

options.text: horizontally, towards the crane
options.feedback: A tension lies along its cable, and this cable hangs vertically.

items.stem: A block is pulled up a rough slope at a steady speed. A student draws its weight, the normal reaction, the tension, friction down the slope and a force labelled 'motion' up the slope. Which arrow should be removed?

options.text: the force labelled 'motion'
options.feedback: Motion is not a force. The pull up the slope is the tension, already drawn.

options.text: friction down the slope
options.feedback: The block slides up a rough slope, so friction down the slope belongs.

options.text: the normal reaction
options.feedback: The block presses on the slope, so the slope pushes back.

options.text: the tension
options.feedback: The rope pulls the block, so its tension is a real force. The invented one is the 'motion' arrow.

items.stem: A candidate draws every force in the right place but puts no arrowheads on the lines. What happens?

options.text: marks are lost, because a line without an arrowhead does not say which way the force acts
options.feedback: A force is a vector; the arrowhead is how the direction is written down.

options.text: nothing is lost, because the positions are right
options.feedback: The reports return to this every year: no arrowhead, no direction, no mark.

options.text: only the weight needs an arrowhead
options.feedback: Every force needs one, and every force needs a label as well.

options.text: the labels can replace the arrowheads
options.feedback: A label names the force and gives its size. The arrowhead gives its direction.

parts.stem:
A book of mass $3$ kg rests on a smooth horizontal table.

Write down the weight of the book.

Answer ________ N
hints: Weight is $mg$.
This paper takes $g = 10$ m/s².
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= mg = 3 \times 10 = 30$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass in kilograms. A weight is a force, so it is $3 \times 10 = 30$ N.
That uses $g = 9.8$. Unit 2 takes $g = 10$ m/s², which the front of the paper states, so the weight is $30$ N.
That divides by $g$. Weight is $mg$, so the mass is multiplied by 10, not divided by it.

context.setting: An incomplete diagram of a sledge

parts.stem:
A sledge is pulled along rough ground by a rope. A student's force diagram shows the weight, the tension in the rope and the force due to friction.

Which force has been left out?

options.text: the normal reaction
options.feedback: The sledge is in contact with the ground, so the ground pushes back at right angles to it.

options.text: a second tension
options.feedback: One rope gives one tension. A second would need a second rope.

options.text: the mass of the sledge
options.feedback: Mass is not a force, so it never appears as an arrow.

options.text: the acceleration
options.feedback: An acceleration is not a force. Only pushes and pulls go on the diagram.

scheme.for: the normal reaction named

hints: Count the contacts, then count the reactions.
parts.workedSolution: The sledge touches the ground, so the normal reaction acts on it. That is the force the diagram is missing.

parts.stem:

Which force does not act on the parcel?

options.text: friction
options.feedback: Smooth means the surface offers nothing along itself, so no friction is drawn.

options.text: the weight

options.feedback: The parcel is in contact with the chute, so the chute pushes back.

options.text: none: all three act
options.feedback: Friction on a smooth surface is an invented force, and inventing one costs a mark.

scheme.for: friction named as the force that does not act

hints: Read the word describing the surface.
parts.workedSolution: The chute is smooth, so there is no force due to friction. Only the weight and the normal reaction act.

The diagram shows a crate held at rest on a slope by a rope. The slope is smooth.

State what this tells you about the forces acting on the crate.

accepted: there is no friction on the crate
no force due to friction acts

scheme.for: no force due to friction acts

hints: Which force needs a rough surface?
parts.workedSolution: A smooth surface exerts nothing along itself, so there is no friction on the crate: only the weight, the reaction and the tension act.

figures.alt: A sledge of mass 15 kg on rough ground pulled by a rope at 22 degrees above the ground with a force of 65 N. R points up, 150 N points down, and arrow (i) points horizontally backwards.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows a sledge of mass $15$ kg being dragged over rough ground by a rope at $22°$ to the ground.

Name the force marked (i).

scheme.for: the arrow named as the force due to friction

hints: The ground is rough and the sledge is moving forwards.
parts.workedSolution: The sledge moves forwards over rough ground, so friction acts backwards along the ground. The arrow marked (i) is the force due to friction.

commonErrors.feedback: The tension in the rope is the 65 N arrow already drawn. A backwards force along rough ground is friction.
The reaction is the arrow labelled $R$, at right angles to the ground. This one lies along it.

parts.stem:
The force due to friction on the sledge is $6.2$ N per kg of mass.

Calculate the force due to friction.

Answer ________ N
hints: Per kilogram of mass means multiply by the mass in kilograms.
parts.workedSolution: Friction $= 6.2 \times 15 = 93$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the rate itself. It gives $6.2$ N for every kilogram, so it is multiplied by the $15$ kg.
That multiplies by the weight, $150$ N. The rate is given per kilogram of mass, so it is multiplied by $15$.

figures.alt: A suitcase of mass 15 kg on a rough horizontal floor, pulled by a strap at 32 degrees above the floor with a force of 90 N. Three further arrows are marked: (i) straight up, (ii) horizontally backwards, and (iii) straight down.

parts.stem:
A suitcase of mass $15$ kg is pulled along a rough horizontal floor by a strap. The strap makes an angle of $32°$ with the floor and the pull along it is $90$ N.

Three of the forces acting on the suitcase are marked on the diagram.

Name the force marked (i).

scheme.for: the arrow named as the normal reaction

hints: The suitcase is in contact with the floor.
parts.workedSolution: The floor pushes the suitcase straight up out of its surface, so (i) is the normal reaction.

commonErrors.feedback: The strap's pull is the 90 N arrow. The upward force at right angles to the floor comes from the floor itself.
The weight pulls downwards, towards the Earth. This arrow points away from the floor.

parts.stem: Name the force marked (ii).

scheme.for: the arrow named as the force due to friction

hints: The floor is rough and the suitcase moves forwards.
parts.workedSolution: The floor is rough and the suitcase moves forwards, so friction acts backwards along the floor: (ii) is the force due to friction.

commonErrors.feedback: The reaction leaves the floor at right angles and is marked (i). This arrow lies along the floor.
The strap pulls forwards at 32°, not backwards along the floor.

parts.stem:
Write down the weight of the suitcase.

Answer ________ N
hints: Weight is $mg$.
This paper takes $g = 10$ m/s².
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= mg = 15 \times 10 = 150$ N, and that is the force marked (iii).

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass in kilograms. A weight is a force, so it is $15 \times 10 = 150$ N.
That uses $g = 9.8$. Unit 2 takes $g = 10$ m/s², which the front of the paper states, so the weight is $150$ N.
That divides by $g$. Weight is $mg$, so the mass is multiplied by 10, not divided by it.

parts.stem: State why the normal reaction on the suitcase is smaller than its weight.

accepted: Part of the pull acts upwards and holds up part of the weight, so the normal reaction is smaller than the weight.
The strap has a vertical component, which supports some of the weight, so the reaction is less than the weight.

any: part of the pull acts upwards
holds up part of the weight
holds up some of the weight
does not support all of the weight
does not have to support the whole weight

scheme.for: the strap is at an angle, so part of the pull acts upwards
so the floor supports less than the whole weight and the reaction is smaller

hints: The strap is not horizontal.
What is left for the floor to hold up?
parts.workedSolution: The strap is at an angle, so part of the pull acts upwards. The floor then has less to hold up, and the normal reaction is smaller than the weight.

commonErrors.feedback: On a horizontal floor with no other vertical force the reaction does equal the weight. Here the strap pulls partly upwards, so it does not.

parts.stem: Which one of these should not appear on the force diagram for the suitcase?

options.text: the mass of the suitcase, in kilograms
options.feedback: A force diagram carries forces only, and a mass is not a force.

options.text: the normal reaction
options.feedback: The suitcase touches the floor, so the reaction belongs there.

options.text: the force due to friction
options.feedback: The floor is rough and the suitcase moves, so friction acts.

options.text: the pull of the strap
options.feedback: The strap pulls the suitcase, so its tension is one of the forces.

scheme.for: the mass identified as the entry that does not belong

hints: Which of the four is measured in kilograms?
parts.workedSolution: Mass is measured in kilograms and is not a push or a pull, so it never appears as an arrow on a force diagram.

figures.alt: A box of mass 12 kg on a rough slope inclined at 26 degrees, sliding down it. Three arrows are marked: (i) at right angles to the slope, (ii) straight down, and (iii) along the slope.

parts.stem:
A box of mass $12$ kg is released from rest on a rough slope inclined at $26°$ to the horizontal and slides down it.

The three forces acting on the box are marked (i), (ii) and (iii) on the diagram.

Name the force marked (i).

scheme.for: the arrow named as the normal reaction

hints: It leaves the slope at right angles.
parts.workedSolution: The slope pushes the box straight out of its own surface, so (i) is the normal reaction.

commonErrors.feedback: The weight is vertical, and on a slope that is not the same as perpendicular to the surface. It is marked (ii).
Friction lies along the slope, not at right angles to it.

parts.stem: Name the force marked (iii).

scheme.for: the arrow named as the force due to friction

hints: The slope is rough and the box slides down it.
parts.workedSolution: The box slides down the rough slope, so friction acts up it: (iii) is the force due to friction.

commonErrors.feedback: Nothing is attached to the box, so there is no string and no tension.
The reaction is at right angles to the slope and is marked (i). This arrow lies along the slope.

parts.stem:
Write down the weight of the box.

Answer ________ N
hints: Weight is $mg$.
This paper takes $g = 10$ m/s².
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= mg = 12 \times 10 = 120$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass in kilograms. A weight is a force, so it is $12 \times 10 = 120$ N.
That uses $g = 9.8$. Unit 2 takes $g = 10$ m/s², which the front of the paper states, so the weight is $120$ N.
That divides by $g$. Weight is $mg$, so the mass is multiplied by 10, not divided by it.

parts.stem:
The box is now dragged back up the slope at a steady speed.

State the direction in which the force due to friction on the box then acts, and give a reason.

accepted: Down the slope, because friction opposes the motion of the box.
It acts down the slope, since friction opposes the sliding.

any: opposite to the direction of motion

scheme.for: down the slope
because friction opposes the motion

hints: Which way is the box moving now?
parts.workedSolution: The box now moves up the slope, and friction opposes the motion, so the friction acts down the slope.

commonErrors.feedback: Up the slope is the way the box is now going. Friction works against the sliding, so it turns round with the motion and acts down the slope.

parts.stem:
The force due to friction on the box is $5.5$ N per kg of mass.

Calculate the force due to friction.

Answer ________ N
hints: Per kilogram of mass means multiply by the mass.
parts.workedSolution: Friction $= 5.5 \times 12 = 66$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the rate on its own. It gives $5.5$ N for every kilogram, so multiply it by the $12$ kg.
That multiplies by the weight, $120$ N. The rate is per kilogram of mass, so the multiplier is $12$.

On the block on the table, arrow (i) points up, (ii) points down, T points towards the pulley and (iii) points away from it. On the hanging block, (iv) points up and W points down.

parts.stem:
A block of mass $7$ kg is kept still on a rough level table. A light inextensible string joins it over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table to a block of mass $11$ kg hanging freely, as shown.

Name the force marked (i).

scheme.for: the arrow named as the normal reaction

hints: Which body is resting on a surface?
parts.workedSolution: The block on the table is pushed straight up by the table, so (i) is the normal reaction.

commonErrors.feedback: The tension acts along the string, towards the pulley, and is already labelled $T$.
The weight of that block acts downwards and is marked (ii).

parts.stem: Name the force marked (iii).

scheme.for: the arrow named as the force due to friction

hints: The table is rough, and the string pulls the block towards the pulley.
parts.workedSolution: The table is rough and the string pulls the block towards the pulley, so friction acts away from the pulley: (iii) is the force due to friction.

commonErrors.feedback: The tension pulls the block towards the pulley. This arrow points the other way, along a rough surface, so it is friction.
The reaction is at right angles to the table and is marked (i).

parts.stem: Name the force marked (iv), which acts on the hanging block.

scheme.for: the arrow named as the tension

hints: The hanging block touches nothing.
parts.workedSolution: The string pulls the hanging block upwards, so (iv) is the tension, with the same label $T$ as the other end.

commonErrors.feedback: A reaction needs a surface, and the hanging block touches none. The upward pull is the string's.
Friction needs a rough surface in contact. The hanging block has neither.

parts.stem:
Write down the weight of the $7$ kg block.

Answer ________ N
hints: Weight is $mg$.
This paper takes $g = 10$ m/s².
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= mg = 7 \times 10 = 70$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass in kilograms. A weight is a force, so it is $7 \times 10 = 70$ N.
That uses $g = 9.8$. Unit 2 takes $g = 10$ m/s², which the front of the paper states, so the weight is $70$ N.
That divides by $g$. Weight is $mg$, so the mass is multiplied by 10, not divided by it.

parts.stem: The string is light and the pulley is smooth. State what this tells you about the tension at the two ends of the string, and give a reason.

accepted: The tension is the same at both ends, because the string is light and the pulley is smooth.
It is the same at both ends, since a light string over a smooth pulley carries one tension.

scheme.for: the tension is the same at both ends
because the string is light and the pulley is smooth

hints: What would change the tension along the string?
parts.workedSolution: A light string over a smooth pulley carries one tension throughout, so the tension is the same at both ends and one label $T$ serves for both.

commonErrors.feedback: Different tensions belong to different strings. This is one string, light, over a smooth pulley, so the tension does not change along it.

parts.stem:

figures.alt: A trolley of mass 20 kg held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at 18 degrees by a rope lying along the slope. Arrow (i) leaves the trolley at right angles to the slope, (ii) points straight down, and T points up the slope.

parts.stem:
A trolley of mass $20$ kg is held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at $18°$ to the horizontal by a rope lying along the slope.

Name the force marked (i).

scheme.for: the arrow named as the normal reaction

hints: It leaves the slope at right angles.
parts.workedSolution: The slope pushes the trolley straight out of its surface, so (i) is the normal reaction.

commonErrors.feedback: The weight is vertical, and this arrow is at right angles to a tilted surface, so the two are not the same.
The rope lies along the slope and its tension is already labelled $T$.

parts.stem: Name the force marked (ii).

scheme.for: the arrow named as the weight

hints: Which arrow is vertical?
parts.workedSolution: The arrow points straight down towards the Earth, so (ii) is the weight of the trolley.

commonErrors.feedback: The reaction is at right angles to the slope and is marked (i). A vertical arrow on a slope is the weight.
The slope is smooth, so there is no friction at all.

parts.stem:
Calculate the weight of the trolley.

Answer ________ N
hints: Weight is $mg$.
This paper takes $g = 10$ m/s².
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= mg = 20 \times 10 = 200$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass in kilograms. A weight is a force, so it is $20 \times 10 = 200$ N.
That uses $g = 9.8$. Unit 2 takes $g = 10$ m/s², which the front of the paper states, so the weight is $200$ N.
That divides by $g$. Weight is $mg$, so the mass is multiplied by 10, not divided by it.

parts.stem: Which list gives exactly the forces acting on the trolley?

options.text: the weight, the normal reaction and the tension
options.feedback: Three forces: the Earth pulls, the slope pushes at right angles, and the rope pulls along the slope.

options.text: the weight, the normal reaction, the tension and friction
options.feedback: The slope is smooth, so there is no friction. An invented force costs a mark.

options.text: the weight and the tension
options.feedback: The trolley rests on the slope, so the slope pushes back. The reaction is the commonest omission of all.

options.text: the weight, the normal reaction, the tension and the component of the weight down the slope
options.feedback: That component is part of the weight, which is already listed. Counting it again counts the same pull twice.

scheme.for: the three forces listed exactly, with nothing extra

hints: Work round the trolley: Earth, surface, rope, sliding.
parts.workedSolution: The Earth gives the weight, the slope gives the normal reaction and the rope gives the tension. The slope is smooth, so there is no friction and nothing else acts.

parts.stem: The slope is smooth. State what this tells you about the force the slope can exert on the trolley, and name the force that is therefore not drawn.

accepted: The slope can only push at right angles to itself, so there is no friction on the trolley.
The surface exerts no force along itself, so no force due to friction acts.

scheme.for: the slope can push only at right angles to itself
so no force due to friction is drawn

hints: Which force needs a rough surface?
parts.workedSolution: A smooth slope can only push at right angles to itself: it exerts nothing along its surface. So there is no friction, and only the weight, the normal reaction and the tension are drawn.

context.setting: A box sliding up a rough slope, then back down

parts.stem:
A box of mass $19$ kg is sliding up a rough slope inclined at $25°$ to the horizontal, with nothing attached to it.

Write down the weight of the box.

Answer ________ N
hints: Weight is $mg$.
This paper takes $g = 10$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass in kilograms. A weight is a force, so it is $19 \times 10 = 190$ N.
That uses $g = 9.8$. Unit 2 takes $g = 10$ m/s², which the front of the paper states, so the weight is $190$ N.
That divides by $g$. Weight is $mg$, so the mass is multiplied by 10, not divided by it.

parts.stem: Which list gives exactly the forces acting on the box while it slides up the slope?

options.text: its weight, the normal reaction, and friction down the slope
options.feedback: Nothing pulls it: it is still moving up, so friction acts down the slope, against the sliding.

options.text: its weight, the normal reaction, and friction up the slope
options.feedback: Friction opposes the sliding. The box slides up, so friction points down the slope.

options.text: its weight, the normal reaction, friction down the slope, and a force up the slope keeping it moving
options.feedback: Nothing touches the box to push it up the slope; it is slowing down. A force of motion is invented.

scheme.for: weight, normal reaction, friction down the slope

hints: Which way is it sliding? Friction points the other way.
Is anything touching it that could push it up the slope?
parts.workedSolution: The weight acts vertically down and the normal reaction at right angles to the slope. The box slides up, so friction acts down the slope. Nothing pushes it up the slope: it is slowing down.

parts.stem: The box stops, then slides back down the slope. In which direction does the force due to friction act on it now?

options.text: up the slope
options.feedback: It now slides down, so friction turns round and acts up the slope. Nothing else changes.

options.text: down the slope, as before
options.feedback: Friction faces the sliding, and the sliding has turned round.

options.text: there is no friction once it has stopped
options.feedback: It is sliding again, over a rough surface, so friction acts, against the new motion.

scheme.for: up the slope

hints: Which way is it sliding now?
parts.workedSolution: The box now slides down the slope, so friction acts up the slope. The weight and the normal reaction are as before.

questions.solutionProgram: W = 19 * 10; up: W, R, F down the slope; back down: F up the slope

context.setting: The same box on three different slopes

parts.stem:
A box is at rest on a rough slope, with nothing attached to it.

Which list gives exactly the forces acting on the box?

options.text: its weight, the normal reaction, and friction up the slope
options.feedback: Without friction the box would slide down, so friction acts up the slope and holds it.

options.text: its weight and the normal reaction only
options.feedback: On a rough slope something must stop it sliding down: that is friction, up the slope.

options.text: its weight, the normal reaction, and friction down the slope
options.feedback: The box would slide down, so friction points up the slope, against that.

scheme.for: weight, normal reaction, friction up the slope

hints: Which way would it slide if the slope were smooth?
parts.workedSolution: The weight acts down, the reaction at right angles to the slope, and friction up the slope, stopping the box sliding down.

parts.stem:
The box is pushed up a smooth slope by a force parallel to the slope.

Which list gives exactly the forces acting on the box?

options.text: its weight, the normal reaction, and the push up the slope
options.feedback: Smooth means no friction, so three forces act: the weight, the reaction and the push.

options.text: its weight, the normal reaction, the push, and friction down the slope
options.feedback: A smooth slope gives no friction, so none is drawn.

options.text: its weight, the normal reaction, the push, and a force down the slope
options.feedback: The pull down the slope is part of the weight, already drawn. It is not a force of its own.

scheme.for: weight, normal reaction, the push

hints: Read the word describing the slope.
parts.workedSolution: The slope is smooth, so there is no friction: the weight, the normal reaction and the push up the slope.

parts.stem:
The push is removed and the box slides back down the smooth slope.

Which list gives exactly the forces acting on the box?

options.text: its weight and the normal reaction
options.feedback: Nothing pushes and nothing grips: only the weight and the reaction are left.

options.text: its weight, the normal reaction, and friction up the slope
options.feedback: The slope is still smooth, so there is still no friction.

options.text: its weight, the normal reaction, and the push, now down the slope
options.feedback: The push was removed. Moving down the slope does not need a force down the slope.

scheme.for: weight and normal reaction

hints: What is still touching the box?
parts.workedSolution: Only the Earth and the smooth slope act on it: the weight and the normal reaction.

questions.solutionProgram: rough, at rest: W, R, F up; smooth, pushed up: W, R, push; smooth, sliding down: W, R

context.setting: A plank on two supports with a sack hanging from one end

parts.stem:
A uniform plank AB, of mass $30$ kg and length $5$ m, rests horizontally on two supports, one at A and one at C, where AC $= 3.5$ m. A sack of mass $23$ kg hangs from B on a light rope.

Write down the size of the force that the rope exerts on the plank at B.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: $230$ N, the weight of the sack

hints: The rope holds the sack up. How hard must it pull?
The rope pulls down on the plank just as hard as it pulls up on the sack.
parts.workedSolution: The rope holds the sack still, so it pulls with the sack's weight, $23 \times 10 = 230$ N, and it pulls down on the plank at B with the same 230 N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass in kilograms. A weight is a force, so it is $23 \times 10 = 230$ N.
That uses $g = 9.8$. Unit 2 takes $g = 10$ m/s², which the front of the paper states, so the weight is $230$ N.
That divides by $g$. Weight is $mg$, so the mass is multiplied by 10, not divided by it.

parts.stem: Where does the weight of the plank act?

options.text: at its midpoint, $2.5$ m from A
options.feedback: Uniform means its mass is spread evenly, so its weight acts at the middle of the plank.

options.text: halfway between the supports, $1.75$ m from A
options.feedback: The supports do not decide where the weight acts. The 2019 report saw exactly this: the weight put midway between the supports.

options.text: at C, over the support
options.feedback: The weight acts at the plank's midpoint, wherever the supports are.

scheme.for: at the midpoint

hints: What does uniform tell you?
parts.workedSolution: A uniform plank's weight acts at its midpoint: $5 \div 2 = 2.5$ m from A.

parts.stem:
How many forces act on the plank?

Answer ________

scheme.for: 4: the weight, the reaction at A, the reaction at C and the rope's pull at B

hints: Work round the plank: the Earth, each support, and each rope.
parts.workedSolution: The plank's weight, a reaction at each of the two supports, and the rope's pull at B: four forces.

commonErrors.feedback: Each support pushes up with its own reaction, so there are two reactions, one at A and one at C.
The sack's weight acts on the sack. The plank feels it only as the rope's pull at B, which is counted already.

parts.stem: The plank is taken off its supports and hung horizontally from two vertical ropes, one at each end. How should the tensions in the two ropes be labelled?

options.text: with two different letters, one for each rope
options.feedback: Two ropes carry two tensions, which need not be equal, so each gets its own letter.

options.text: both $T$, because the ropes are the same
options.feedback: The 2019 report saw this. Two ropes carry two tensions, which are only equal if the load is central.

options.text: both 150 N, half the plank's weight each
options.feedback: The sack hangs at one end, so the ropes do not share the load equally.

scheme.for: two different letters

hints: One string over a smooth pulley has one tension. How many strings are there here?
parts.workedSolution: Two separate ropes carry two tensions, so they take two letters, such as $T_1$ and $T_2$.

questions.solutionProgram: rope's pull at B = 23 * 10; weight at the midpoint, 2.5 m from A; forces: weight, R at A, R at C, pull at B

context.setting: A student's force diagram with one arrow too many

parts.stem:
A sledge of mass $28$ kg is pulled up a rough slope inclined at $12°$ to the horizontal at a steady speed by a rope parallel to the slope.

Write down the weight of the sledge.

Answer ________ N
hints: Weight is $mg$.
This paper takes $g = 10$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass in kilograms. A weight is a force, so it is $28 \times 10 = 280$ N.
That uses $g = 9.8$. Unit 2 takes $g = 10$ m/s², which the front of the paper states, so the weight is $280$ N.
That divides by $g$. Weight is $mg$, so the mass is multiplied by 10, not divided by it.

parts.stem:
Aoife draws five arrows on the sledge: its weight, $280$ N, vertically down; the normal reaction at right angles to the slope; the tension up the slope; friction down the slope; and an arrow labelled "resultant force" up the slope.

Which arrow should be removed?

options.text: the resultant force
options.feedback: The resultant is what the forces add up to, not a force of its own; at a steady speed it is zero anyway.

options.text: friction down the slope
options.feedback: The sledge slides up a rough slope, so friction down the slope belongs.

options.text: the normal reaction
options.feedback: The sledge presses on the slope, so the slope pushes back at right angles.

scheme.for: the resultant force

hints: Which arrow is not a push or a pull from something touching the sledge, or from the Earth?
parts.workedSolution: Every force comes from the Earth or from something touching the sledge. The resultant is the total of those four, so it is removed.

parts.stem: The sledge is then pulled up an icy slope, which is smooth, at a steady speed. Which other arrow must also go from Aoife's diagram?

options.text: friction
options.feedback: A smooth surface gives no friction, so its arrow goes.

options.text: the normal reaction
options.feedback: Smooth or rough, the slope still pushes back on the sledge.

options.text: the tension
options.feedback: The rope still pulls, so the tension stays. It is friction that a smooth slope cannot give.

scheme.for: friction

hints: Read the word describing the new slope.
parts.workedSolution: Smooth means no friction, so the friction arrow goes; the weight, reaction and tension stay.

questions.solutionProgram: W = 28 * 10; remove 'resultant force'; smooth: remove friction

context.setting: A box pulled over a rough floor, its pull already drawn

parts.stem:
A box of mass $26$ kg is pulled along a rough horizontal floor by a rope at $35°$ above the floor. The diagram already shows the 90 N pull of the rope.

How many other forces must be marked on the diagram?

Answer ________

scheme.for: 3: the weight, the normal reaction and friction

hints: Work round the box: Earth, floor, rope, sliding. Which one is drawn already?
parts.workedSolution: The Earth gives the weight, the floor the normal reaction, and the sliding over a rough floor friction. The rope's pull is printed already: three more forces.

commonErrors.feedback: The floor is rough and the box slides, so friction must be marked too.
The pull is printed already. Drawing it again adds a force that is not there.

parts.stem:
Write down the weight of the box.

Answer ________ N
hints: Weight is $mg$.
This paper takes $g = 10$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass in kilograms. A weight is a force, so it is $26 \times 10 = 260$ N.
That uses $g = 9.8$. Unit 2 takes $g = 10$ m/s², which the front of the paper states, so the weight is $260$ N.
That divides by $g$. Weight is $mg$, so the mass is multiplied by 10, not divided by it.

parts.stem: In which direction does the force due to friction act on the box?

options.text: horizontally, opposite to the way the box moves
options.feedback: Friction lies along the floor and against the sliding.

options.text: along the rope, backwards
options.feedback: Friction acts along the surface the box slides on, which is the floor, not the rope's line.

options.text: horizontally, the way the box moves
options.feedback: That is the direction of motion. Friction opposes it.

scheme.for: along the floor, against the motion

hints: Friction lies along the surface. Which surface does the box slide on?
parts.workedSolution: Friction acts along the floor, opposite to the motion of the box.

questions.solutionProgram: other forces: W, R, F (3); W = 26 * 10; friction backwards along the floor
