figures.alt: Block P, of mass 32 kg, on a rough horizontal table, joined by a light string over a smooth pulley at the table's edge to block Q, of mass 27 kg, hanging freely.

parts.stem:
Block P, of mass $32$ kg, lies on a rough horizontal table. A light inextensible string joins it over a smooth pulley at the edge of the table to block Q, of mass $27$ kg, which hangs freely. The system is released and Q falls.

Write down the weight of Q.

Answer ________ N
hints: Weight is $mg$.
This paper takes $g = 10$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass in kilograms. A weight is a force, so it is $27 \times 10 = 270$ N.
That uses $g = 9.8$. Unit 2 takes $g = 10$ m/s², which the front of the paper states, so the weight is $270$ N.
That divides by $g$. Weight is $mg$, so the mass is multiplied by 10, not divided by it.

parts.stem:
The force due to friction on P is $4.5$ N per kg of its mass.

Calculate the force due to friction on P.

Answer ________ N
hints: Per kilogram of mass: multiply by the mass, not the weight.
parts.workedSolution: Friction $= 4.5 \times 32 = 144$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the rate itself. It gives $4.5$ N for every kilogram, so it is multiplied by the $32$ kg.
That multiplies by the weight, $320$ N. The rate is per kilogram of mass, so it is multiplied by $32$.

parts.stem: Which list gives exactly the forces acting on P while Q is falling?

options.text: its weight, the normal reaction, the tension towards the pulley, and friction away from the pulley
options.feedback: The Earth, the table, the string and the sliding each give one force.

options.text: its weight, the normal reaction, the tension towards the pulley, and friction towards the pulley
options.feedback: P slides towards the pulley, so friction acts the other way, away from it.

options.text: its weight, the tension and friction
options.feedback: P rests on the table, so the table pushes up on it: the normal reaction. The 2025 report saw it left off.

scheme.for: weight, normal reaction, tension, friction away from the pulley

hints: Work round P: Earth, table, string, sliding.
parts.workedSolution: P has its weight down, the normal reaction up, the tension towards the pulley and friction away from it.

parts.stem: Which list gives exactly the forces acting on Q while it is falling?

options.text: its weight and the tension
options.feedback: Q touches nothing but the string, so only the Earth and the string act on it.

options.text: its weight, the tension and a normal reaction
options.feedback: Q hangs freely and touches no surface, so there is no reaction. The 2025 report saw an extra reaction here.

options.text: its weight, the tension and friction
options.feedback: Friction needs a surface to slide on, and Q touches none.

scheme.for: weight and tension

hints: What is Q touching?
parts.workedSolution: Q hangs freely, so only its weight and the tension act on it.

parts.stem:
Q hits the floor and does not rebound, so the string goes slack. P keeps sliding across the table.

How many forces act on P now?

Answer ________

scheme.for: 3: weight, normal reaction and friction

hints: A slack string cannot pull.
parts.workedSolution: The slack string no longer pulls, so the tension goes. P keeps its weight, the normal reaction, and friction, since it still slides: three forces.

commonErrors.feedback: A slack string cannot pull, so the tension is no longer there.
P is still sliding over a rough table, so friction still acts.

parts.stem: State the direction of the force due to friction on P while it keeps sliding, and give a reason.

accepted: Away from the pulley, because P is still sliding towards the pulley and friction opposes the sliding.
Backwards, opposite to its motion, because it is still moving and friction acts against the motion.

any: opposite to the way it moves

scheme.for: away from the pulley (opposite to the motion)
because P is still sliding and friction opposes the sliding

hints: Which way is P still moving?
parts.workedSolution: Away from the pulley, because P is still sliding towards the pulley and friction opposes the sliding.

commonErrors.feedback: Towards the pulley is the way P is moving. Friction acts against the sliding, away from the pulley.

parts.stem:
Calculate the size of the normal reaction on P while it keeps sliding.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: vertically, only the weight and the reaction act, and P does not rise or sink, so they balance

hints: Which forces on P are vertical now?
P does not rise or sink, so those forces balance.
parts.workedSolution: Only the weight and the reaction are vertical, and P neither rises nor sinks, so $R = 32 \times 10 = 320$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the mass in kilograms. A weight is a force, so it is $32 \times 10 = 320$ N.
That uses $g = 9.8$. Unit 2 takes $g = 10$ m/s², which the front of the paper states, so the weight is $320$ N.
That divides by $g$. Weight is $mg$, so the mass is multiplied by 10, not divided by it.

questions.solutionProgram: W_Q = 27 * 10; F = 4.5 * 32; P: W, R, T, F; Q: W, T; slack: W, R, F (3), friction away from the pulley; R = 32 * 10

findTheMistake.stem: Orla lists the forces on a box of mass $7$ kg sliding down a rough slope inclined at $30°$. Her list:
studentWorking: the weight, $70$ N, down the slope
the normal reaction $R$, at right angles to the slope
the force due to friction $F$, up the slope
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 tilts the weight with the slope. The Earth pulls straight down whatever the surface does, so the $70$ N arrow is vertical; only its component, $70\sin 30° = 35$ N, lies along the slope.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three entries are right, which keeps the first mark for the diagram. The Earth pulls straight down on a slope just as it does on the flat, so the weight arrow is vertical. The part of the weight that runs down the slope is a component: work it out beside the diagram when you start resolving.

findTheMistake.stem: Cormac labels the forces on a block of mass $8$ kg resting on a rough table and pulled by a horizontal string. His labels:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 labels a force with a mass. Kilograms measure how much matter there is; the arrow shows the pull of the Earth on it, which is $8 \times 10 = 80$ N.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three arrows are named correctly, so the first of the two diagram marks stands. Every label on a force diagram is a force, in newtons. If a mass appears in the question, multiply it by $10$ before it goes on the picture.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh describes the forces on a crate resting on a slope inclined at $25°$ to the horizontal. Her description:
studentWorking: the normal reaction acts vertically upwards
the rope's tension acts up the slope
the slope is smooth, so no friction acts
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 points the reaction the wrong way. A surface pushes straight out of itself, so on a slope the reaction is at right angles to the slope, not to the ground. Only on a horizontal surface are the two the same.
correction: the normal reaction acts at right angles to the slope
findTheMistake.feedback: Three of the four statements are right, which keeps the first diagram mark. Picture the crate pressing into the surface: the push that stops it comes straight back out, perpendicular to the surface it is resting on.

prompts.prompt: What must every force on a force diagram carry?
prompts.answer: An arrow showing the direction it acts in, and a label naming it or giving its size.

prompts.prompt: How do you work out the weight of a body of mass $m$ kg on this paper?
prompts.answer: Weight = mg, and Unit 2 takes g = 10, so a mass of 6 kg has a weight of 60 N.

prompts.prompt: In which direction does the weight of a body act?
prompts.answer: Vertically downwards, from the centre of the body, whatever the surface underneath is doing.

prompts.prompt: In which direction does the normal reaction on a body act?
prompts.answer: At right angles to the surface the body rests on, pointing away from that surface.

prompts.prompt: In which direction does friction act on a body that is sliding?
prompts.answer: Along the surface, opposite to the direction the body is sliding.

prompts.prompt: A light string passes over a smooth pulley. What can be said about the tension at its two ends?
prompts.answer: It is the same at both ends, so one label serves for both.

prompts.prompt: A box rests on a slope. Which two forces are most often left off the diagram?
prompts.answer: The normal reaction and the force due to friction.

prompts.prompt: Why is the pull down a slope not drawn as a separate force?
prompts.answer: It is part of the weight, which is already drawn: its components are working, not forces.

prompts.prompt: How many normal reactions act on a block resting on one flat surface?
prompts.answer: One: a single contact gives a single normal reaction.

prompts.prompt: What is wrong with labelling an arrow on a force diagram $12$ kg?
prompts.answer: Kilograms measure mass, not force. The label should be the weight, 120 N.

findings.asked: Forces on a block; resolve vertically; F = ma.
findings.wentWrong: A frictional force was invented, labels and arrows were missing; many did not see vertical equilibrium and wrote two-term equations such as R = 17 sin 33; sine and cosine swapped; g omitted; mass used as weight. In the F = ma part most reached '= 5.8a', but some multiplied the acceleration by the weight rather than the mass.
findings.rule: Resolve perpendicular to the motion: every vertical force appears in the equilibrium equation; F = ma uses the mass, never the weight.

findings.asked: Mark the forces on a suspended rod.
findings.wentWrong: Tensions given the same letter; forces or arrows missing; given forces omitted; reactions added; the rod's weight placed midway between the strings instead of at the centre.
findings.rule: A uniform rod's weight acts at its midpoint; each string gets its own tension label.

findings.asked: 'Show that' an acceleration; forces on a block; F = ma with a changed mass.
findings.wentWrong: Working backwards from the given acceleration scored nothing; R was the commonest omission; friction given a fixed value; arrows and labels missing; the mass change (6 kg to 8 kg) missed; sin/cos swapped; equilibrium assumed.
findings.rule: Derive the acceleration from the forces; the normal reaction is always on the diagram.

findings.asked: Forces on a block with a pulling force at an angle; then motion.
findings.wentWrong: Reaction written as 50 with no resolving, or as 30 sin 37; some diagrams had no forces at all; the zero acceleration in part (ii) was not understood.
findings.rule: Mark every force before writing an equation, even if not asked.

findings.asked: Forces on an inclined plane; 'show that' an acceleration; deceleration.
findings.wentWrong: Acceleration substituted rather than derived; weight not drawn vertically; an extra force down the slope; weight components on the diagram were tolerated.
findings.rule: Weight is vertical; its components are your working, not extra forces.

findings.asked: Label the forces on two connected blocks.
findings.wentWrong: Only about half got the diagram: tensions the wrong way, friction missing or reversed, no normal reaction on one block, an extra reaction on the other, and weights labelled with masses (no g).
findings.rule: Weight = mg; friction opposes motion; one normal reaction per surface contact.

findings.asked: Force diagram on a slope; resolve; F = ma.
findings.wentWrong: Friction direction wrong, normal reaction omitted, extra forces, missing arrows - fundamental errors at the end of the paper; sin/cos confusion was less frequent than before.
findings.rule: Two marks for a correct diagram are the cheapest in the paper - draw it properly.

insight.ruleToRemember: Every force is an arrow with a label: weight mg vertically down from the centre, normal reaction perpendicular to the surface, friction along the surface against motion, tension along each string with its own label - and nothing else.
insight.aStarSignal: A clean diagram for a two-body or inclined system that leads straight to correct resolving and F = ma, with 'show that' results derived rather than checked.

checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-c before writing)
checks.detail: Further Mathematics Unit 2, untiered, calculator paper. Identifying and labelling every force on a body: weight mg vertically down, the normal reaction at right angles to each surface in contact, the tension along each string, and friction along a rough surface against the sliding, on horizontal planes, on inclined planes and for two bodies joined over a smooth pulley. No coefficient of friction, no limiting equilibrium, no air resistance and no three-dimensional work.

checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-c before writing)
checks.detail: The Unit 2 sheet gives F = ma, the four constant-acceleration formulae, the magnitude of xi + yj, the angle between xi + yj and i, and the quadratic formula. It does not give W = mg, so the weight relationship and g = 10 m/s² are recall and are listed in mustKnow.

checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-c before writing)
checks.detail: Command words from packs/further-maths/exam-true/command-words.json: Identify (with its alias State, typical 1 mark), Write down (typical 1), Calculate (typical 3, min 2). checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-c before writing)
checks.detail: packs/further-maths/exam-true/tariffs.json FM2: per-question median 8 marks and 90th percentile 13; per-part median 2 and 90th percentile 4. The diagram parts in the papers are 2 marks for the whole picture (Summer 2025 Q4(i), Q5(i), Q6(i); Summer 2024 Q4(iii); Summer 2023 Q4(i)), scored as any half of the forces then the rest; here each force named is its own 1-mark part, and the four exam-style questions come to 6, 7, 7 and 7 marks. Time allowance is marks x 1.2 minutes.

checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-c before writing)
checks.detail: Every weight is m x 10 computed in the generator: 3 kg gives 30 N, 4 kg 40 N, 5 kg 50 N, 6 kg 60 N, 7 kg 70 N, 8 kg 80 N, 9 kg 90 N, 11 kg 110 N, 12 kg 120 N, 13 kg 130 N, 15 kg 150 N, 16 kg 160 N, 20 kg 200 N and 25 kg 250 N; the sledge figure takes its mass and weight from the stem's 15 kg. checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass; every value computed in scratchpad/fm2-batch-c before writing)
